:::{#exm-noninformative-censoring}
#### Administrative censoring

A trial enrolls patients at a steady rate over two years
and ends four years after the first enrollment,
so each patient's censoring time $C$ is the time from their enrollment to the end of the study,
$C \sim \text{Uniform}(2, 4)$ years.
Enrollment dates are set by the recruitment calendar, not by patients' prognoses,
so $T \ind C$;
the censoring parameters $\theta_C = (2, 4)$ are unrelated to the event-time parameters,
so censoring is non-informative (@def-noninformative-censoring).

Suppose $T \sim \text{Exponential}(\haz)$ with $\haz = 0.2$ per year,
and a patient enrolled 3 years before the end of the study is still event-free at the end,
so $(y, d) = (3, 0)$.
The patient's likelihood contribution is

$$
\ba
\Lik(3, 0)
&= \sb{\p(T=3,C> 3)}^0 \cdot \sb{\p(T>3,C=3)}^{1}
&& \text{(likelihood of $(Y, D)$ with $d = 0$)}
\\
&= \p(T>3,C=3)
&& \text{($x^0 = 1$ and $x^1 = x$)}
\\
&= \p(T>3)\,\p(C=3)
&& \text{(independence of $T$ and $C$)}
\\
&= \surv_T(3)\,\pdf_C(3)
&& \text{(definitions of $\surv_T$ and $\pdf_C$)}
\\
&= \ef{-0.2 \cdot 3} \cdot \frac{1}{4 - 2}
&& \text{(exponential survival function, uniform density)}
\\
&= \ef{-0.6} \cdot 0.5
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\\
&\approx 0.5488 \cdot 0.5
&& \text{($\ef{-0.6} \approx 0.5488$)}
\\
&\approx 0.2744.
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\ea
$$

The factor $\pdf_C(3) = 0.5$ does not involve $\haz$,
so it does not affect which value of $\haz$ maximizes the likelihood.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-informative-censoring}
#### Informative censoring (counterexample)

Suppose half of a cohort is frail, with event time $T = 1$ year,
and half is robust, with $T = 5$ years.
Frail patients become too sick to attend follow-up visits
and drop out at $C = 0.5$ years,
while robust patients stay in the study until it ends at $C = 10$ years.
Then $\Pr(C = 0.5 \mid T = 1) = 1$ but $\Pr(C = 0.5 \mid T = 5) = 0$,
so $T$ and $C$ are dependent and censoring is informative.

The true probability of surviving past 2 years is
$\surv_T(2) = \Pr(T > 2) = 0.5$.
Everyone still under observation just after $0.5$ years is robust,
so if we treated the dropouts as representative of the patients still under observation,
as independence would justify,
we would compute

$$
\ba
\Pr(T > 2)
&= \Pr(T > 0.5) \cdot \Pr(T > 2 \mid T > 0.5)
&& \text{(chain rule; $\cb{T > 2} \subseteq \cb{T > 0.5}$)}
\\
&\approx 1 \cdot \Pr(T > 2 \mid T > 0.5,\ C > 0.5)
&& \text{(no events before 0.5; treat dropouts as representative)}
\\
&= 1 \cdot 1
&& \text{(all observed patients past 0.5 are robust)}
\\
&= 1,
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\ea
$$

which overstates the true value $0.5$.
:::
